plan.contextChunk: This figure contains four sub-panels (a through d) showing the different matrix representations used to encode a graph for graph neural networks. Panel a) depicts a 6-node undirected graph with nodes labeled 1 through 6, connected by edges whose identities are marked by the pair of endpoint node labels (e.g., ‘1\3’, ‘1\4’, ‘2\3’, ‘3\4’, ‘3\6’, ‘4\5’, ‘5\6’). Panel b) shows the adjacency matrix A (N × N), a square binary matrix encoding which pairs of nodes are connected by edges. Panel c) shows the node feature matrix X (D × N), in which each column stores the D-dimensional feature vector associated with one of the N nodes. Panel d) shows the edge feature matrix E (Dᴷ × E), in which each column stores the Dᴷ-dimensional feature vector associated with one of the E edges, with edges ordered to match the labeled pairs in panel a). Labels for each matrix include its name, symbol, and dimensions. This figure introduces the three standard data structures—adjacency matrix, node feature matrix, and edge feature matrix—that together fully represent a graph with node and edge attributes in a deep learning context.

interactionPlan.concept: A graph with node and edge attributes is fully encoded by three tensors — the adjacency matrix A, the node feature matrix X, and the edge feature matrix E — and the indexing bijection (node i ↔ row/column i of A and column i of X; edge e ↔ column e of E) is what lets a graph neural network consume the graph as arrays.
elements: panel label 'a)' with 6-node undirected graph
node circles labeled 1,2,3,4,5,6 (brown/orange outline)
per-node vertical stack of colored squares = node feature vector (orange/brown palette), one beside each node
per-edge vertical stack of colored squares = edge feature vector (teal/green palette), one beside each edge
panel label 'b)' with title 'Adjacency matrix, A' and dimension 'N × N' (teal text)
6×6 grid for A with row and column headers 1..6; filled steel-blue cells at symmetric positions for each edge, empty white cells otherwise
panel label 'c)' with title 'Node data, X' and dimension 'D × N' (brown text)
5×6 grid for X with column headers 1..6; each column a node's feature vector in orange/brown shades
panel label 'd)' with title 'Edge data, E' and dimension 'D_E × E' (teal text)
4×7 grid for E with two-row column headers giving endpoint pairs 1/3,1/4,2/3,3/4,3/6,4/5,5/6; each column an edge's feature vector in teal/green shades
highlight overlays: selected node's row+column outline in A and column outline in X; selected edge's column outline in E plus rings on its two endpoint nodes

interactions.teaches: Clicking node i reveals the indexing bijection for nodes: the same index i picks out row i AND column i of the adjacency matrix A (its connections) and column i of the node data matrix X (its features) — one graph node, one position in each matrix.

Clicking an edge reveals the indexing bijection for edges: that edge's feature vector is exactly one column of E (ordered by its endpoint pair), and the same click rings the two nodes the edge joins in panel a, linking the edge column back to the two node indices.

interactions.label: Focus representation
interactions.teaches: Stepping the focus through each panel shows that the picture (a) and the three matrices (b,c,d) are the same object in different encodings: A stores only connectivity, X stores per-node attributes, E stores per-edge attributes — none alone is the graph, together they are.

demo_steps.title: The graph as data
demo_steps.narration: Panel a is a 6-node graph where every node carries a feature vector (the orange stack beside it) and every edge carries a feature vector (the teal stack beside it). This attributed graph is the object we must hand to a neural network as arrays.

demo_steps.title: Connectivity → adjacency matrix A
demo_steps.narration: Focus panel b: A is a 6×6 binary matrix with a filled cell exactly where an edge exists. Click any node in panel a and watch its row and column light up in A — those filled cells are precisely that node's neighbours.

demo_steps.title: Node attributes → matrix X
demo_steps.narration: Focus panel c: each column of X is one node's feature vector, in node order. Click a node in panel a and its matching column in X is outlined — the orange stack you saw beside the node IS that column.

demo_steps.title: Edge attributes → matrix E
demo_steps.narration: Focus panel d: each column of E is one edge's feature vector, ordered by endpoint pair (1/3, 1/4, …). Click an edge in panel a and its column in E is outlined while its two endpoint nodes are ringed, tying the edge column back to two node indices.

demo_steps.title: Three matrices = one graph
demo_steps.narration: Return to all panels. A, X and E together fully specify the attributed graph; the row/column indexing is the bridge that turns nodes and edges into tensor positions a GNN can iterate over.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The graph and the three matrices are the same object: a node's index is its row/column in A and its column in X, and an edge's index is its column in E — this indexing bijection is what converts a graph into tensors a network can process.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Lay out four panels left-to-right labeled a), b), c), d). Panel a: place nodes roughly as in the source (2 top-left, 1 top-center, 4 top-right, 3 mid-left, 5 mid-right, 6 bottom-center) with brown-outlined white circles and slate-blue edges for the seven pairs listed. Beside each node draw a short vertical stack of orange/brown squares (its feature vector); beside each edge a vertical stack of teal/green squares (its edge feature vector). Panel b: 6×6 grid, steel-blue filled cells at the symmetric edge positions, white elsewhere, headers 1..6 on top and left, teal title 'Adjacency matrix, A / N × N'. Panel c: 5-row × 6-column grid of orange/brown shaded cells, column headers 1..6, brown title 'Node data, X / D × N'. Panel d: 4-row × 7-column grid of teal/green shaded cells with two-line column headers showing endpoint pairs, teal title 'Edge data, E / D_E × E'. On node click, draw a bold outline around that node's row and column in A and its column in X; on edge click, outline that edge's column in E and ring its two endpoint nodes in panel a. When panelFocus selects a single panel, dim the others to ~30% opacity but keep them visible so cross-panel highlights still read; highlighted elements always render at full opacity.

discrepancies: Node feature vector colors are randomly generated (seeded PRNG) rather than matching the specific color patterns visible in the source figure; however, consistency between panel a stacks and panel c columns is maintained
Node positions differ from the source layout (e.g., source has node 2 higher and more to the left, node 3 more centered); topology is preserved but spatial arrangement is approximate
In the source, node feature stacks are positioned variably (above, beside) depending on node location; generated code always places them to the right of the node circle
Panel titles use sans-serif font instead of the serif/math italic style seen in the source (e.g., 'Adjacency matrix, A' with italic A)
The overall horizontal compression in the rendered screenshot makes panels b–d appear smaller and more cramped than in the source figure
evaluation.notes: The 4-panel structure, graph topology (7 edges, 6 nodes), adjacency matrix, and matrix dimensions are all correctly implemented; the click-to-highlight interactions linking nodes/edges to their matrix representations are pedagogically excellent and conceptually accurate, though feature vector colors are procedurally generated rather than matching the source's specific palette.
action_items: Adjust node positions to more closely match the source layout (node 2 higher-left, node 3 more centered, node 6 lower-center) for better visual fidelity
Use serif/italic font for panel titles and mathematical notation (A, X, E, N×N, D×N, D_E×E) to match the source's typographic style
Consider hardcoding the feature vector colors to match the source figure's specific patterns rather than using seeded random generation
